1 1.
The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.

The accused no.1 is stated to be the vendor of accused no.4 partnership firm, of which accused no.1,
2 and 3 were the partners, from where the food article, that is, 'Sugar Boiled Confectionery' was lifted for sampling.

Accused no.5 Company is stated to be the manufacturer / supplier from whom the vendor had purchased the food article and accused no.6 is stated to be its Nominee.
2.

As per the complaint, on 18.07.2006, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Gian Chand and Field Assistant (FA) J. P. Bhardwaj under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Yogesh Pratap reached along with their staff at the premises of accused no.4 at 48-UA (5994), Jawahar Nagar, Delhi-07, where the accused no.1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.

The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Sugar Boiled Confectionery' from the vendor that was lying in sealed packets of 440 gram each bearing identical label declaration, to which he agreed.
A sample of three such sealed packets was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.

Each sample was separately packed, fastened,
marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.
Vide report dated 08.08.2006, the PA found the sample to be misbranded on the ground that it gave misleading declaration regarding the presence of some colors.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
It was found that accused no.4 Firm had three partners as accused no.1, 2 and 3 (since discharged).

It was found that the sample had been purchased by them from accused no.5 company, of which one Sh. S. C. Sawhney was the nominee on the day of sampling but he expired on 08.10.2006, and accused no.6 was the nominee at the manufacturing unit.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.
The complaint was then filed in the court on 12.01.2007 alleging violation of section 2(ix)(e) and (g) of PFA Act, read with rule 37 of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned.

The accused appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 28.02.2007, opining the sample to be not conforming to the standards on the ground that it contained permitted synthetic colour more than the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm.

4. In the meanwhile, on an application moved under section 294 CrPC, vide order dated 24.04.2009, the accused no.1 to 4 were given the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act on the basis of an admitted invoice and they were discharged.
Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1.

Rajender Kumar on 22 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/132614592/
2
5. Based on the CFL report, pre charge evidence was led wherein PW1 FI Gian Chand was examined by the prosecution.

Based on his testimony, charge was framed against accused no.5 and 6 on 19.02.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ix)(g) and (k) of PFA Act read with Rule 30 of PFA Rules, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
6. Before proceeding ahead, it is pertinent to note that there is inherent defect in the charge so framed, though no such defect has been pointed out by any side.

Violation of Rule 30 of PFA Rules amounts to violation of section 2(ia)(j) of PFA Act which is punishable under section 16(1)(1A) of PFA Act under the offence of "adulteration" and it would not be a case of violation of section 2(ix)(g)
and (k) of PFA Act which pertains to the offence of "misbranding".

It appears that though the findings of the CFL report were noticed by the court at that time, yet the applicable sections were mentioned in the charge on the basis of the PA report and those mentioned in the complaint.
Irrespective of that, the court shall deal with the matter on both the counts.
7. At the trial, prosecution examined three witness in support of its case.
PW-1 FI Gian Chand, PW-2 Sh. Yogesh Pratap and PW-3 FA J. P. Bhardwaj were a part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

They deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 18.07.2006 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 3 sealed packets of 440 gram each of 'Sugar Boiled Confectionery', separately sealing, marking the sample bottles,
and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, cash memo Ex. PW1/A1, notice Ex. PW-1/B, panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, notice under section 14A Ex. PW1/D, raid report Ex. PW-2/A, PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/E and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/F.
PA report Ex. PW- 1/G was received and investigation was started.

Letters Ex. PW-1/H to Ex. PW1/M2 pertain to the correspondence between the FI, the accused persons and the government agencies to ascertain their constitution and role during the course of investigation.
After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/N was taken from the Director PFA.
The complaint Ex. PW-1/O was filed in the court.

A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex.
PW-1/P was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/Q.

These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that representative sample was not taken or that the label declaration was not identical on all the packets or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated.

8. Statements of the accused no.5 (through AR) and accused no.6 under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 15.09.2012 wherein they denied the knowledge about the sample proceedings but claimed that the reports of analysts were not reliable being at variation.
They chose to lead evidence in defence.
9. Accused no.6 examined himself as DW-1 as the only defence witness.
He informed that he was nominee of the manufacturing unit of the company in 1996 but vide subsequent resolution dated 29.04.2000 Ex. DW-1/A, his previous nomination stood superseded.
He stated that the nominee for Delhi region was Mr. S. C. Sawhney who not be implicated due to his death.
Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1.

sentences.text:
Rajender Kumar on 22 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/132614592/
3 10.

It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against both the accused no.5 and 6 beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 28.02.2007 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
11. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various missing links in the testimony of the witnesses.

Ld. 
Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore, conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report.
He has relied upon the various judgements in his support.
12. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused persons and have carefully perused the material available on record.

13. It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused persons is for violation of section 2(ix)(g) and (k) of the PFA Act on the basis of the findings of the CFL report with respect to presence of colors in excess of prescribed maximum limit.
Section 2(ix)(g) and (k) pertain to the offence of misbranding where there is some misleading or false or deceptive statement or the product is not labelled as per the PFA Rules.
However, it would be seen that such an opinion was given only by the PA and not by the CFL.
The CFL report nowhere gives any opinion as to any such misleading or deceptive statement or violation of any labelling rules.

If the findings of CFL are to be considered, then that would be a violation of Section 2(ia)(j) of PFA Act because the food article contained synthetic colors in excess of the prescribed limit as given in Rule 30 of PFA Rules.
14. As per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.
As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and conclusive evidence for the facts stated therein.
Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.

15. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.
16.

entities.text: Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents.

entities.text: Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Director is a greater expert and therefore the statute says that his certificate shall be accepted by the court as conclusive evidence.
For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director....
Superseded is a strong word.
It means obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal.

4 certificate supersedes the report given by the public analyst.
Once superseded it does not survive for any purpose.
It will be anomalous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded."
17. Since the report of CFL is final and conclusive and the same supersedes the report of PA, only this report has to be considered and the report of PA has to be ignored.

However, the defence strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. Ramesh Chand [2010 (2) JCC 1250], Food Inspector v. Parvinder Malik [2014(2) FAC 306], State v. Vinod Kumar Gupta [2010(2) JCC 957], State v. Virender Kohli [2014(2) FAC 223], State v. Kamal Aggarwal [2014(2) FAC 183], State v. Vidya Gupta [2014(1) FAC 291], State v. Dinesh Goswami [2014(1) FAC 302], State v. Mahabir [2014(1) FAC 286], State v. Santosh Sharma [2014(1) FAC 296], Raja Ram Seth & Sons v. Delhi Administration [2012(2) FAC 523], State v. Sunil Dutt [2011(4)
JCC 2377] and State v. Rama Rattan Malhotra [2012(2) FAC 398].

sentences.text: It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative.

18. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'.

Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation.

19. Therefore, it can be safely said that though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.
If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative or there is possibility that they were not of the same lot or batch, he would get benefit on that count.
20. Well, the differences between the two reports would show substantive variations in the two reports.
The PA never found any deficiency in the nature, substance or quality of the food article in question.
It was as per the prescribed standards as given in Item No. A.25.01 of Appendix B of PFA Rules.

entities.text: Item No. A.25.01 of Appendix B
entities.label: PROVISION

sentences.text: The only opinion given by the PA was with respect to the label declarations, as it was stated that the label showed presence of five food colors but only one color was present in the sample.
The analytical values determined by the PA showed that the synthetic color found in the sample was Carmosine which was present upto 22.81 ppm, and well within the prescribed limit of 100 ppm.
21. On the other hand, the CFL Certificate is in complete variation to the findings of PA.
The CFL report nowhere points towards any deficiency or violation in the labelling rules or standards.
It has been specifically mentioned that the label complied with the provisions of the PFA Rules.
No opinion has been given to the effect that the declarations on the label were inconsistent with the ingredients of the food article.
No misleading or deceptive or false statement was found by the CFL on the label of the product.
Thus, the CFL report negated the findings of the PA report on the sole count on which the prosecution was launched.
Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1.

Rajender Kumar on 22 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/132614592/
5 22.

The ground on which the CFL opined the sample to be not conforming to the standards was the presence of synthetic coloring matter Carmosine, which it found to be present upto the extent of 119.26 ppm, which was beyond the prescribed maximum limit of 100 ppm.
Apparently, no such finding was there in the sample analyzed by the PA where the extent of color was found only upto 22.81 ppm.

23. Such huge variation in the two reports would force the court to take a view that the two samples were not representative or were not of the same lot / batch or were not bearing identical label declarations.
Some minor variations can be ignored in the two reports on account of different test methodology or the equipments used.
But such huge variation in the quantity of color cannot be explained easily.
Synthetic color upto 22.81 ppm on 08.08.2006 would not have sharply increased upto 119.26 ppm by 28.02.2007.
Even after lapse of very long period of time, there is hardly any change in the nature of quantity of synthetic food colors, unlike the natural colors which are prone to change with passage of time.
It was for the prosecution to explain the said variation in the two reports, even if the CFL report is final as to the findings therein.
The rule that CFL report supersedes the PA report would apply only if the samples are representative.
If the samples analyzed by the PA and CFL are of different food article, then the court cannot ignore the PA report and still hold that the CFL report would be final.

Therefore, considering the huge variation in the two reports, not only the point of adulteration but also on the point of misbranding, it can be said that the samples were not representative or were of different lot / batch or having different label declarations.
24. In view of the above discussion, the accused persons are entitled to be given benefit of doubt.

The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the sample in question was 'misbranded' or 'adulterated' within the meaning of section 2(ix) or 2(ia) of PFA Act and thus, no case would be made out against the accused persons for commission of offences punishable under section 7/16 of the PFA Act.
25.
Having said so, both the accused no.5 and 6 are acquitted of the charges.

However, the bail bond of accused no.6 shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A. CrPC.
26. File be consigned to record room.
